title: Advances and Evolving Challenges in Spinal Deformity Surgery
condition_or_topic: Surgical correction of adult spinal deformity (ASD)
clinical_background: ASD comprises varied thoracolumbar abnormalities associated with trauma, progression of earlier spinal conditions, or degeneration. Its prevalence reaches up to about 70% in elderly patients. Non-operative treatments are generally used first; surgery is considered when pain, disability, neurological symptoms, or worsening curvature persist despite such care. Although surgical planning and techniques have advanced, selecting patients and procedures, achieving sufficient correction, and preventing complications remain challenges.
objectives: Characterize advances in surgical techniques for ASD correction and identify areas requiring improvement.

Review developments in pre-operative planning, open surgery, and minimally invasive approaches, together with contributors to morbidity after correction and barriers to adopting newer spinal procedures.
study_design: Literature review using PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Google Scholar to examine advances in surgical correction of adult spinal deformity (ASD) and challenges affecting outcomes from patient and clinician perspectives. The review considers preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative phases.

population.description: People with adult spinal deformity (ASD) discussed in the reviewed literature.

interventions: Open surgical procedures for ASD correction
Minimally invasive surgery (MIS) approaches for ASD correction
interpretation: The review concludes that standardized assessment, three-dimensional planning, more tailored and staged operations, minimally invasive techniques, improved osteotomies, navigation, and newer implants have expanded surgical options for adult spinal deformity (ASD). Their potential to provide durable symptom relief is still constrained by patient-selection difficulties, insufficient or excessive correction, and complications including blood loss, infection, hardware failure, PJK/PJF, and pseudarthrosis. The authors consider stronger clinical evidence and further technological development necessary to improve outcomes.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: The cited evidence does not support a uniform advantage for minimally invasive surgery. Several studies found similar disability scores, spinopelvic measurements, and complication rates with cMIS and open correction at one year, whereas a study with longer follow-up reported significantly fewer major complications after cMIS. Studies of staged surgery also differed: one reported significantly less hardware failure than with unstaged open correction, while another found no significant difference between staged and unstaged cMIS. Earlier minimally invasive approaches corrected sagittal parameters less than open surgery; more complex approaches such as cMIS have addressed some, but not all, of that concern. Studies cited by the authors associate age-adjusted alignment goals and selected implant or augmentation strategies with improved mechanical outcomes, although the extent of supporting evidence varies.
clinical_implications: Radiographic measurements and classification systems can help relate spinal alignment to disability, establish correction targets, and inform the choice of operation; patient age and other characteristics affect how those targets should be interpreted.

Three-dimensional imaging, physical models, computational risk estimates, and intraoperative navigation may improve planning, implant placement, and preoperative counseling, but their effect on ASD-specific clinical outcomes is not fully established.
Selected patients with mild to moderate deformity may benefit from more limited correction, while severe deformity can require more extensive surgery with greater potential morbidity.
Low bone density can compromise fixation and increase the risk of hardware failure and revision surgery. Implant designs and augmentation strategies may help address particular mechanical risks.
PJK radiographic findings may not fully reflect symptoms; pain, neurological findings, and persistent disability are relevant when considering revision surgery.
Undercorrection is associated with poorer health-related quality of life, and younger patients may require more substantial correction for functional improvement.
The benefits of minimally invasive approaches remain variable across patients and deformity patterns, particularly when extensive correction is needed.
practice_implications: Individualize operative planning and radiographic correction goals according to patient age, deformity characteristics, and health status rather than relying on alignment targets alone.
Use patient and deformity characteristics to guide selection between minimally invasive and open techniques; the review describes MISDEF2 as one approach to this selection.
Consider limited fusion for appropriate patients with small radiographic changes and good sagittal balance, while weighing the potential benefits and logistical demands of staged correction.
Address surgical-site infection risk through optimization of comorbidities, timely antibiotics, sterile operative technique, and postoperative wound care.
Consider measures discussed for limiting operative blood loss, including tranexamic acid; the reported effectiveness of positioning strategies is variable.
When assessing possible revision for PJK, account for symptoms and functional consequences as well as imaging findings.
For selected complex or high-risk ASD operations, operating-room arrangements that permit collaboration between two surgeons may be beneficial.
limitations: Reported radiographic and clinical outcomes after minimally invasive correction are heterogeneous, and clinical validation of these approaches remains needed.
The effectiveness of minimally invasive surgery, and the frequency of conversion to open surgery, remain uncertain for certain severe deformities or large fusion masses.
The clinical utility of stereoradiography remains under investigation despite encouraging measurement accuracy.
Validated trials have not yet established how intraoperative navigation methods affect operative performance and clinical outcomes specifically in ASD correction.
Few validated measures identify which clinically complex patients can tolerate and benefit from major correction.
The Boachie-Adjei classification does not link its categories to symptoms or direct treatment decisions, and there is no consensus on which patients with PJK should undergo revision.
Additional clinical evidence is needed to determine the long-term effect of investigated grafts and biological materials on fusion.
open_questions: Which patients obtain the greatest clinical benefit from minimally invasive rather than open correction, especially when deformity is severe?
Which patient groups benefit from staged procedures, and what logistical obstacles affect their use?
How can risk stratification and preoperative health optimization improve outcomes for frail or otherwise clinically complex patients?
How should the need for revision be determined in patients with PJK when imaging findings and symptoms do not align?
Do newer imaging and navigation techniques improve ASD-specific clinical outcomes in validated trials?
What are the long-term effects of investigated grafts and biological materials on successful fusion?
future_directions: Evaluate three-dimensional motion analysis alongside conventional radiographic measurements to better characterize spinal mechanics and correction needs.
Develop patient-specific implants, including rods intended to reduce fracture and hardware failure.
Investigate real-time modeling, simulation, and augmented reality for intraoperative implant placement.
Apply machine and deep learning to patient identification, risk stratification, and management algorithms that incorporate health status and comorbidities.
Generate comprehensive outcome data and validated clinical trials, including comparisons of minimally invasive and open techniques, to guide procedure selection.
Improve approaches to severe deformity while reducing infection, blood loss, mechanical failure, PJK/PJF, and pseudarthrosis.

tables.summary: The scale assigns scores across neurological findings, focal pain, instrumentation problems, kyphosis change, changes at the uppermost instrumented vertebra, and junctional level. The article reports validation against quality of life, pain, and likelihood of revision surgery. PLC denotes posterior ligamentous complex, UIV denotes uppermost instrumented vertebra, and VAS denotes visual analog scale.

main_conclusion: The authors conclude that advances in assessment, modeling, operative techniques, navigation, and implants have expanded surgery for adult spinal deformity. Further progress depends on better patient selection and age-appropriate correction, stronger evidence for minimally invasive approaches, and fewer major complications, supported by comprehensive outcomes data and validated trials.
narrative_summary:
This review examined developments and persistent challenges in surgery for adult spinal deformity (ASD), drawing on literature identified through PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Google Scholar. The authors describe how standardized radiographic measures, three-dimensional modeling, and computational risk prediction can inform operative planning. Minimally invasive approaches, limited fusions, staged procedures, refinements in osteotomy, intraoperative navigation, and newer implants offer ways to tailor correction or improve procedural safety. However, reported outcomes with minimally invasive surgery vary, and its effectiveness for certain severe deformities remains uncertain; the authors call for clinical trials comparing it with open surgery.

Patient selection, insufficient correction—particularly when age is not considered—and complications remain substantial concerns. The review reports surgical site infection in up to 10% of ASD procedures and hardware failure in up to about 50% in some cohorts. PJK/PJF occurs in between 20 and 40% in most studies, while pseudarthrosis occurs at approximately 6%; these figures describe different complications and study populations. The authors also discuss blood loss and the risk of revision surgery. For clinical planning, they emphasize assessment of individual alignment targets, comorbidities, bone health, and procedural risks. They conclude that sustained improvement in symptoms and quality of life will require more comprehensive outcome evidence, validated trials, and continued technical development.

main_findings.context: Thresholds come from cited studies, not a new analysis in this review.

main_findings.description: A cited analysis found that younger patients needed more extensive deformity correction than older patients to improve symptoms.
main_findings.context: The analysis evaluated disability across age and SRS-Schwab strata.

main_findings.description: A cited evaluation found that incorporating body mass index and bone density improved the predictive performance of the GAP score.
main_findings.context: Comparison was with the unadjusted GAP score; no numerical performance estimate is supplied.

main_findings.description: Studies found that stereoradiography measured spinal anatomy accurately compared with CT reconstruction, particularly for scoliosis and sagittal measurements.
main_findings.context: Its clinical utility and effect on care remain under investigation.

main_findings.description: Studies reported better operative planning with physical three-dimensional spine models, especially for complex or anomalous anatomy.

main_findings.description: Studies reported more accurate screw placement and shorter operations with patient-specific guides made by three-dimensional printing.

main_findings.context: The review does not give effect estimates for these variables.

main_findings.description: Published predictive models for PJK, PJF, and pseudarthroses identified patient age, vertebral locations, implant types, and pre-operative radiographic measurements as important features.
main_findings.context: These are findings from cited modeling studies.

main_findings.description: Published radiographic findings for cMIS are heterogeneous, although the approach appears capable of correcting sagittal imbalance even in severe ASD.
main_findings.context: The review characterizes clinical outcomes relative to open surgery as ranging from unchanged to improved.

main_findings.description: Several studies found comparable disability scores and spinopelvic measurements after cMIS and open correction, without a difference in complication rates.
main_findings.context: The comparison applies to patients in the cited studies at this follow-up point.

main_findings.description: A study with longer follow-up reported a significantly lower incidence of major complications after cMIS.
main_findings.context: The comparison was with open correction and included PJK/PJF, pseudarthroses, and hardware failure; no numerical incidence or p value is reported.

main_findings.description: Studies of patients with mild to moderate deformity, small radiographic changes, and satisfactory sagittal balance found fewer perioperative complications with fusion confined to the affected region.

main_findings.description: One study reported significantly less hardware failure with staged correction than with unstaged open deformity correction.

main_findings.description: Another study found no significant difference between staged and unstaged cMIS procedures.

main_findings.description: Randomized trials of endoscopic discectomy demonstrated non-inferiority to open alternatives and reported less intraoperative bleeding, shorter hospital stays, and faster recovery.
main_findings.context: These cited trials concern discectomy; their results are not presented as validated specifically for ASD correction.

notable_adverse_events: Surgical site infection after ASD surgery: reported in up to 10% of cases; prior infection at the site and elevated body mass index were identified as risk factors.

Hardware failure after ASD surgery: reported at rates ranging up to about 50% in some cohorts; described forms include rod fracture, painful or prominent implants, screw breakage, and screw loosening.
PJK/PJF after ASD surgery: incidence reported to be between 20 and 40% in most studies; a majority of patients with PJK developed clinically significant signs within 18 months after surgery.
Pseudarthrosis after ASD correction: approximately 6%; recurrent pseudarthrosis after revision affected up to 50% of patients.
Other reported cardiac complications of ASD surgery include myocardial infarction and cardiac arrest; rates are not given.
Other reported pulmonary complications of ASD surgery include pneumonia and pulmonary embolism; rates are not given.
Deep vein thromboses are reported among vascular complications of ASD surgery; a rate is not given.
Cauda equina and nerve root injury are reported among neurological complications of ASD surgery; rates are not given.
Sepsis, superficial infection, and thrombophlebitis are listed among infectious complications of ASD surgery; separate rates are not given.

Increased exposure to blood products and large fluid shifts during ASD surgery can lead to transfusion-associated reactions and severe coagulopathies with multi-organ consequences; rates are not given.

Major complications comprising PJK/PJF, pseudarthroses, and hardware failure had a significantly lower incidence after cMIS than after open correction in one cited study with longer follow-up; rates are not given.

subgroup_analyses: A cited age-stratified analysis found that younger patients had lower PT, PI-LL mismatch, LL-TK mismatch, and SVA thresholds for significant disability and poor health-related quality of life than older patients; the review indicates that younger patients likely need more extensive correction.
Patients with more severe ASD or associated disability were described as benefiting most from surgical correction, without a subgroup-specific effect estimate.

In patients with mild to moderate deformity, small radiographic changes, and good sagittal balance, studies associated short fusion limited to the deformity with fewer perioperative complications; no rate is given.

One study found significantly less hardware failure for staged versus unstaged open correction, whereas another found no significant difference between staged and unstaged cMIS; neither numerical comparison is supplied.

A study with longer follow-up found significantly fewer major complications with cMIS than with open correction, whereas several studies reported no difference in complications at one year post-operatively.
The review identifies low bone density as a factor associated with poor implant stability, difficult fixation, hardware failure, and greater revision risk; no subgroup-specific rates are given.
secondary_results: CT-based reconstruction was reported to depict bony abnormalities and support measurement of pedicle diameter and spinal angles; low-dose stereoradiography generated three-dimensional representations from two-dimensional images while limiting radiation.

The MISDEF2 protocol uses deformity flexibility and PI-LL mismatch, SVA, PT, and coronal Cobb angle to assign patients to four classes intended to guide implant and MIS-versus-open selection; the review provides no validation result for this protocol.

The review describes six anatomic osteotomy grades, from grade 1 to grade 6; more extensive resections can permit greater correction but also increase spinal instability and postoperative complication risk.

PSO and VSR use has declined because of substantial morbidity and high complication rates; cited work indicates that three-dimensional planning and intraoperative navigation can improve the accuracy of bone cuts and provide anatomical feedback.
New pedicle screw designs are described as having the potential to improve fixation in osteoporotic bone; the review does not report a quantified clinical effect.

Studies of S2-alar-iliac screws reported less soft-tissue dissection, easier connection to posterior instrumentation, greater mechanical strength, and fewer reoperations; numerical estimates are absent.
Risk factors identified for PJK include older age, greater sagittal abnormalities, low bone density, fusion to the sacrum or pelvis, and overcorrection of lumbar lordosis.
The Boachie-Adjei system categorizes PJK by failure type, kyphosis degree, and spondylolisthesis but does not link categories to symptoms or direct treatment decisions.

The Hart-International Spine Study Group scale has been validated against health-related quality of life, pain, and revision likelihood, and the review states that it establishes a threshold for considering revision; no threshold value is supplied in the prose.
Risk factors reported for pseudarthrosis include older age, comorbidities, smoking, larger thoracic kyphotic angles, and longer constructs.

For patients with certain severe deformities or large fusion masses, the effectiveness of MIS and its rate of conversion to open surgery remain unknown; the review calls for comparative clinical trial data.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: Surgery is an important option for adult spinal deformity (ASD). The authors reviewed PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Google Scholar to examine advances in correction and persistent challenges from patient and clinician perspectives across pre-, intra-, and post-operative care. Standardized imaging measurements and three-dimensional models support planning. Complex minimally invasive surgery (MIS), focused corrections, and staged operations may individualize treatment while limiting operative time; improved osteotomies, navigation, and implants have also increased safety. Patient-selection differences and insufficient correction contribute to variable outcomes. Blood loss, infection, implant failure, proximal junctional kyphosis/failure, and pseudarthroses remain obstacles. MIS is used increasingly, but its clinical value requires further validation. As ASD becomes more prevalent, durable symptom control will require comprehensive plans that make use of computational and imaging advances.

document_sections.heading: 1. Introduction
document_sections.content: Population aging is accompanied by more spinal disease. ASD affects up to about 70% of elderly patients and includes thoraco-lumbar abnormalities arising after trauma, progression of adolescent idiopathic scoliosis in adulthood, or degeneration such as de novo scoliosis and deformity related to multi-level disc disease. Its combined disability and economic burden have prompted medical and surgical treatments intended to improve symptoms and quality of life. Initial nonsurgical options include physical therapy, aerobic exercise, non-steroidal anti-inflammatories, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, anticonvulsants, and steroid, trigger-point, or nerve root block injections. Procedures are used when nonsurgical care fails in patients with persistent severe pain, substantial physical disability, neurological symptoms, or worsening abnormal curvature. The six broad surgical categories are decompression; decompression with posterior fusion and limited instrumentation; decompression with posterior fusion and lumbar-curve instrumentation; decompression with anterior/posterior fusion; fusion with thoracic instrumentation; and osteotomies. Selection algorithms consider spinal flexibility and imaging measures such as pelvic tilt. Planning, implants, and techniques have evolved, including MIS approaches intended to reduce the morbidity of open correction. Both open and MIS operations still face difficulties involving candidate identification, procedure selection, complications, and the amount of correction attainable. The authors review progress in planning, open operations, and MIS, together with postoperative morbidity and barriers to adopting newer approaches, using PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Google Scholar.

document_sections.heading: 2.1. Radiological Parameters and Scoring Systems
document_sections.content: Measurements from plain radiographs and computed tomography (CT) can stratify pre-operative risk and define correction goals. Posterior–anterior and lateral whole-spine images permit regional assessment with Cobb’s angles for cervical lordosis (CL), thoracic kyphosis (TK), thoracolumbar kyphosis, and lumbar lordosis (LL); sagittal spinopelvic assessment with sagittal vertical axis (SVA), pelvic incidence (PI), pelvic tilt (PT), sacral slope (SS), and T1 pelvic angle; and coronal assessment with scoliosis-curve Cobb’s angles and coronal balance. The validated Scoliosis Research Society (SRS)-Schwab classification combines measures including PI-LL mismatch with coronal and sagittal modifiers to guide treatment. It has shown strong reliability across institutions; PI-LL mismatch <10◦, SVA < 4 cm, and PT < 20◦ predict favorable clinical outcomes, less disability, and better health-related quality-of-life scores. The Global Alignment and Proportion (GAP) score was developed to improve prediction of postoperative mechanical complications and revision risk, which the SRS-Schwab system does not address. Correction targets remain under refinement because age and comorbidities affect classification and outcomes. An earlier analysis across age and SRS-Schwab groups found that younger patients needed more extensive correction for symptomatic improvement. Adjusting GAP for body mass index and bone density improved predictive performance over unadjusted GAP. Quantitative classifications have helped standardize approaches around ASD mechanics, alignment goals, and technique selection.

document_sections.heading: 2.2. Pre-Operative Modeling
document_sections.content: Computational planning tools may improve anticipation of operative difficulties and postoperative complications. Virtual and physical three-dimensional reconstructions aid visualization. CT reconstruction depicts bony abnormalities, including facet defects and osteophyte complexes, and allows precise pedicle-diameter and spinal-angle measurements. Low-dose stereoradiography reconstructs three-dimensional bone anatomy from two-dimensional images in an upright, weight-bearing position while limiting radiation. Compared with CT reconstruction, studies report highly accurate spinal measurements, particularly for scoliosis curvature and sagittal parameters; its clinical usefulness and effect are still being studied despite proof of concept. Physical models printed from virtual reconstructions have improved planning in complex or anomalous anatomy. Three-dimensional printing has also produced patient-specific implant guides associated with more accurate screw placement and shorter surgery. Large ASD datasets support machine- and deep-learning models, including models for perioperative transfusion risk. Post hoc analysis linked greater transfusion risk to operative time, hematocrit, and patient weight. Other models attempt to predict proximal junctional kyphosis (PJK), proximal junctional failure (PJF), and pseudarthroses; identified features include age, lower and upper instrumented vertebral locations, implant type, and pre-operative imaging parameters. Pre-operative complication prediction may improve counseling and help reduce morbidity.

document_sections.heading: 2.3. Minimally Invasive Surgery
document_sections.content: MIS, increasingly used for ASD, seeks to preserve anatomy, reduce morbidity, and speed functional recovery through smaller incisions and endoscopic tools. Its applications include lateral lumbar interbody fusion (LLIF), oblique lumbar interbody fusion (OLIF), transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (TLIF), posterior lumbar interbody fusion (PLIF), anterior lumbar interbody fusion (ALIF), anterior longitudinal ligament (ALL) release, percutaneous screws, and prone/lateral positioning. Circumferential MIS (cMIS) combines anterior support, such as LLIF/OLIF, with percutaneous posterior instrumentation to improve sagittal and spinopelvic correction. Reported imaging results vary, although cMIS appears capable of correcting sagittal imbalance even in severe ASD. Clinical comparisons with open surgery range from unchanged to improved outcomes. Several studies found similar disability scores and spinopelvic measurements at one year post-operatively, without a difference in complication rates. A study with longer follow-up instead found significantly fewer major complications, including PJK/PJF, pseudarthroses, and implant failure, after cMIS. Because reported correction and outcomes vary, the minimally invasive spine deformity surgery 2 (MISDEF2) protocol uses fixed versus flexible deformity, PI-LL mismatch, SVA, PT, and coronal Cobb angle to assign patients to four classes and guide implant and MIS-versus-open selection.

document_sections.heading: 2.4. Limited Fusions and Staged Procedures
document_sections.content: Better techniques and implants permit more localized correction, particularly for mild to moderate deformity. In patients with small radiographic changes and preserved sagittal balance, short fusion restricted to the affected region was associated with fewer perioperative complications, including implant failure. Staged correction similarly aims to limit instrumentation to what is needed: anterior column support is performed first, then symptoms and correction are reassessed before deciding on posterior instrumentation. This approach shortens each period under anesthesia and allows symptom response to be assessed during correction. One study reported significantly less implant failure with staging than with unstaged open correction; another found no significant difference between staged and unstaged cMIS. Further research is needed to identify which patients benefit and what logistical barriers arise.

document_sections.heading: 2.5. Osteotomy
document_sections.content: Osteotomies are important for severe ASD. Improvements in operative equipment and technique have increased their therapeutic utility. The osteotomy classification shown in Table 1 assigns six anatomic grades according to resected structures, from grade 1, the least extensive, to grade 6, the most extensive. Resection of whole vertebrae and discs may be necessary for major correction, but larger resections increasingly destabilize the spine and raise postoperative complication risk. The principal types are posterior column osteotomies, including Smith-Peterson osteotomy (SPO) and Ponte osteotomy; pedicle subtraction osteotomy (PSO); and vertebral column resection (VSR). Posterior column procedures address facets, laminae, and posterior ligaments. PSO and VSR remove bone across three columns and are more technically demanding. Their use has recently declined because of substantial morbidity and high complication rates. For selected patients requiring extensive correction, three-dimensional planning and CT-based or O-Arm intra-operative navigation may make three-column osteotomies safer by improving cut accuracy and providing real-time information about nearby anatomy. Navigation optimization remains important when alternatives are limited.

document_sections.heading: 2.6. Intraoperative Imaging and Robotic Navigation
document_sections.content: Visualization and navigation tools are used in multiple ASD procedures. Endoscopy and video systems give detailed deep-tissue views through the smaller incisions required for MIS. Randomized discectomy trials found spinal endoscopy non-inferior to open alternatives, with less intraoperative bleeding, shorter hospitalization, and quicker recovery; those findings concern discectomy rather than validated ASD correction. Miniature cameras attached to tubular retractors offer another way to improve visualization. Intra-operative three-dimensional CT-guided and augmented-reality imaging can assist pedicle screw placement; real-time assessment has helped detect misplaced screws and reduce revision surgery. Compared with conventional methods, robotic navigation has improved pedicle screw accuracy and reduced imaging-related radiation exposure. It may also assist when pedicles are difficult to access or prior instrumentation is present. Validated trials have not yet established how these navigation approaches affect operative performance or clinical outcomes specifically in ASD correction.

document_sections.heading: 2.7. Hardware
document_sections.content: Implant developments may extend ASD surgery to more patients. Osteopenia and osteoporosis, which often coexist with ASD, complicate anterior support and pedicle screw placement. Low bone density is associated with poorer implant stability and fixation, postoperative failure, and greater revision risk. Expandable, fenestrated cement-injectable, and conical pedicle screws, along with screw anchors, may improve fixation in osteoporotic bone. For longer constructs, newer sacropelvic screws aim to reduce distal screw failure and pseudarthrosis. S2-alar-iliac screws require less soft-tissue dissection, connect more readily to posterior instrumentation, increase mechanical strength, and reduce reoperation rates. Junctional tethers are under investigation for PJK/PJF prevention; earlier studies found woven tethers safe and showed preliminary indications of lower long-term PJK risk. Additional rods can reinforce posterior constructs. Small-cohort studies associated multirod configurations with fewer rod fractures and pseudarthroses than standard two-rod configurations. Implant innovation may help tailor operations to individual anatomy and needs.

document_sections.heading: 3.1. Patient Selection
document_sections.content: Changing demographics and comorbidity patterns make appropriate ASD surgical selection increasingly difficult. Mean age is 70.5 years for de novo scoliosis and 78.3 years for degenerative hyperkyphosis, yet few validated measures predict tolerance of or benefit from major correction. Patients with more severe ASD or related disability still benefit most from surgery. One proposed model combined patient demographics and procedural features to predict bleeding and operative duration. A separate study developed an ASD frailty index and found greater major-complication risk and longer hospitalization among frailer patients. Further work is needed on risk stratification in clinically complex or frail patients and on the effect of pre-operative health optimization.

document_sections.heading: 3.2. Acute Operative Complications
document_sections.content: ASD correction may require multiple approaches, substantial spinal manipulation, and extensive instrumentation, creating considerable acute intra- and post-operative risk. Reported complications include myocardial infarction and cardiac arrest; pneumonia and pulmonary embolism; deep vein thromboses; cauda equina and nerve root injury; and sepsis, superficial infection, and thrombophlebitis. Surgical site infection can cause major morbidity and mortality and has been reported in up to 10% of ASD operations. Prior site infection and elevated body mass index increase its risk. Studies have shown lower infection incidence with combined comorbidity optimization, timely antibiotics, sterile technique, and postoperative wound care. Major blood loss and fluid shifts may expose patients to transfusion reactions and severe coagulopathies with consequences across multiple organs. Intra-operative tranexamic acid has reduced both the need for and volume of postoperative transfusions. Positioning intended to lower intra-abdominal pressure has produced variable bleeding results; approaches examined include Trendelenburg for lower thoracic/lumbar procedures, reverse-Trendelenburg for cervical procedures, abdominal free suspension with a Jackson table/Wilson frame, and jackknife positioning. Bipolar electrocautery and topical agents such as bone wax have also been investigated. Initial findings with point-of-care viscoelastic coagulation monitoring show fewer total blood products administered. Compared with single-surgeon cases, dual-surgeon spinal operations have shown less blood loss and shorter operative times. Staffing and operating-room arrangements that enable two surgeons may therefore help in selected complex or high-risk ASD cases.

document_sections.heading: 3.3. Undercorrection
document_sections.content: Although ASD undercorrection is relatively uncommon, it is associated with poorer health-related quality of life. It often follows sagittal alignment targets that do not account for age. For PT, PI-LL mismatch, LL-TK mismatch, and SVA, studies found that younger patients reported significant disability and poorer health-related quality of life at lower radiographic thresholds than older patients. Younger patients likely need more extensive correction to improve function. Planning and imaging assessment should therefore be individualized for age-related musculoskeletal changes.

document_sections.heading: 3.4. Hardware Failure
document_sections.content: Instrumentation is central to deformity correction, but reported hardware-failure rates vary, reaching up to about 50% in some cohorts. Risk depends on age, bone density, comorbidities, correction complexity, and the number of fused levels. Common problems include rod fracture, painful or prominent implants, screw fracture, and screw loosening. Rod fracture is particularly important because revision is often needed and recovery can be substantially affected. It occurs most often with procedures involving aggressive sagittal correction, including PSO. Multirod constructs and customized rods that allow greater angular bending may improve long-term implant stability.

document_sections.heading: 3.5. Proximal Junctional Kyphosis and Failure
document_sections.content: PJK and PJF involve abnormal kyphotic curvature at the highest instrumented vertebrae. Most studies report an incidence between 20 and 40%, varying with the population and extent of correction. Most patients with PJK develop clinically significant signs within 18 months after surgery, although timing depends on curvature progression or vertebral structural failure. There is no consensus on which patients require surgery; significant pain, neurological findings, or persistent disability prompt consideration of revision. Reported PJK risk factors include older age, marked sagittal abnormalities, low bone density, fusion to the sacrum/pelvis, and excessive lumbar lordosis correction. Because imaging findings do not always match symptoms, classification tools seek to inform evaluation. Table 2 presents the Boachie-Adjei classification by failure type, kyphosis severity, and spondylolisthesis; this system neither correlates findings with symptoms nor directs treatment. Table 3 presents the Hart-International Spine Study Group scale, which grades neurological deficits, pain, instrumentation problems, kyphosis, fracture or movement of upper instrumented vertebrae, and involved level. That scale has been validated against health-related quality of life, pain, and revision likelihood and provides a threshold for considering revision. Several preventive measures have been studied. In a prospective study, pre-operative teriparatide significantly increased bone mineral content and was associated with an almost 70% reduction in bone failure PJK versus no treatment at two years post-surgery. Studies of vertebral cement augmentation found fewer junctional fractures in instrumented spinal models and a significant clinical reduction in PJK incidence. Early tether data showed low rates of symptomatic PJK and revision. Studies found significantly less PJK with hooks than with pedicle screws at upper instrumented sites; hooks were considered better able to accommodate postoperative forces. Age-adjusted spinopelvic goals also helped prevent overcorrection and junctional stress. Preserving posterior tension bands and using fewer implants and more flexible materials may limit PJK progression.

document_sections.heading: 3.6. Pseudarthrosis
document_sections.content: Pseudarthrosis is failure of bone fusion after ASD correction and carries substantial morbidity and cost. Its rate across ASD is approximately 6%, and it accounts for many revision operations. Risk factors include older age, comorbidities, smoking, large thoracic kyphotic angles, and lengthy constructs. Recurrence affects up to 50% of patients even after revision. Grafts and biological materials are being studied to improve healing and implant integration, but more clinical evidence is needed to establish their effect on long-term fusion. Models using patient and operative variables might support planning and counseling for high-risk patients.

document_sections.heading: 3.7. Minimally Invasive Approaches
document_sections.content: MIS broadens treatment options but has limitations when substantial correction is needed. Early ASD applications had difficulty correcting sagittal measures, while open operations achieved greater correction. More complex procedures such as cMIS have addressed some sagittal-plane limitations. Their effectiveness and the frequency of conversion to open surgery remain uncertain for certain severe deformities or large fusion masses. MIS also brings training needs and start-up costs. As devices improve and MIS expands, comparative clinical trials against open surgery are needed to guide procedure selection for particular ASD presentations.

document_sections.heading: 4. Future Directions
document_sections.content: ASD surgery has changed alongside growth in the affected population and rapid technical advances. Combining three-dimensional motion analysis with conventional imaging measurements may better identify spinal mechanics and correction targets. Imaging may also support patient-specific rods that could reduce rod fracture and implant failure. Intra-operative augmented-reality models and simulations may help ensure safe, effective implant placement. More advanced machine- and deep-learning methods may improve patient identification and risk stratification by identifying groups beyond current descriptive categories. Classifications that better represent patient phenotypes could inform management algorithms incorporating health status and comorbidities for more individualized surgery. Progress across these areas will require close collaboration among academic researchers, industry sponsors, and clinicians providing nonsurgical care.

document_sections.heading: 5. Conclusions
document_sections.content: Increasing global ASD prevalence calls for operations that relieve symptoms and maintain correction over time. Advances include standardized pre-operative assessment, three-dimensional spinal models, complex MIS, focused and staged procedures, safer osteotomies, navigation, and improved implants. Remaining priorities are appropriate patient selection, adequate age-specific correction, better MIS options for severe deformity, and reductions in infection, blood loss, implant failure, PJK/PJF, and pseudarthroses. Because ASD surgery can substantially reduce disability and improve quality of life, comprehensive outcome data, validated clinical trials, and continued innovation are important for further progress.
